Nestling Maiasaura peeblesorum emerge from their leathery-shelled eggs at a total length at birth of approximately 41 centimeters [Lb = approximately 41 centimeters], a measurement consistent with the relatively large hatchling size characteristic of hadrosaurids. This initial body dimension is modest compared to the ultimate total length of 900 centimeters [Li = 900 centimeters] attained by fully grown adults, reflecting a dramatic ontogenetic increase in axial skeletal size. The parchment-shelled eggs, each containing a yolk-dependent embryo, were typically deposited in structured nesting colonies, suggesting a degree of parental attendance uncommon among non-avian dinosaurs. Paleohistological analysis of femoral cross-sections from individuals of varying ontogenetic stages indicates that the overall growth trajectory was rapid during early life, with a notable inflection coinciding with the onset of reproductive maturity. The substantial disparity between hatchling and adult dimensions underscores the high energetic demands placed upon juveniles during the initial months of post-hatching development, a phase during which mass-specific metabolic rates would have been elevated. This period of accelerated growth was likely supported by a combination of endogenous yolk reserves and the progressive transition to exogenous feeding on fibrous vegetation, requiring a gut microbiome adapted to the fermentation of tough plant material.

By the end of their first year, juveniles attain a wet weight at 1 yr of 384,000 grams , representing a substantial fraction of their ultimate body size. Continued somatic expansion over subsequent years leads to a wet weight at 8 yr of 2,300,000 grams , indicating that growth remains vigorous well into the sub-adult period. The ultimate wet weight, estimated at 3,500,000 grams [Wwi = 3,500,000 grams] based on extrapolation of asymptotic growth curves fitted to long-bone circumference data, likely represents the maximum attainable body mass under favorable environmental conditions. This value is comparable to the upper size range reported for other large-bodied hadrosaurines from the late Campanian of North America. A growth model incorporating LAG-based age estimates reveals that individuals plateau near this asymptotic mass by approximately ten to twelve years of age, after which incremental increases are negligible. The considerable accumulation of body tissue during the juvenile and sub-adult phases would have required sustained high ingestion rates, with peak food intake likely occurring during the summer months when forage quality was highest.

Gonadal maturation in this species, inferred from the presence of medullary bone deposits in femoral medullary cavities of skeletally immature females, is reached at a wet weight at puberty of 1,632,000 grams [Wwp = 1,632,000 grams]. This physiological milestone is attained after a period of approximately 1,095 days since birth [tp = approximately 1,095 days since birth], based on histological growth ring counts that correlate with the attainment of a critical body mass threshold at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. The timing of this event is consistent with the life-history strategy of a large, long-lived herbivore that invests heavily in somatic infrastructure before diverting resources toward reproduction. Under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species (37 °C [T = 37 °C]), the interval from hatching to reproductive competence is relatively compressed compared to similarly sized extant reptiles, reflecting the rapid growth rates characteristic of hadrosaurs. The precise onset of gametogenesis likely coincided with the first seasonal breeding window following the achievement of this developmental benchmark. Histological evidence suggests that reproductive activity may have been delayed in years of poor forage availability, indicating a degree of phenotypic plasticity in this life-history transition.

Reproductive output in Maiasaura peeblesorum is inferred from nest site demographics and clutch size distributions preserved in the Two Medicine Formation bonebeds. Females deposited between 30 and 40 eggs per nest [N_R_i = between 30 and 40 eggs per nest] in approximately two clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately two clutches per year], yielding an estimated maximum reproduction rate equivalent to approximately 2 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 2 clutches per year] that reflects the energetic constraints of egg production in a large-bodied dinosaur. At the estimated active body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], embryonic development within the incubating egg would have progressed rapidly, with the chorionate embryo utilizing yolk reserves to sustain growth until hatching. The total lifespan, based on maximum longevity estimates from cortical bone remodeling patterns, extends to approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years] under typical ecological conditions, though some individuals may have survived beyond this age in the absence of predation or disease at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. This lifespan is intermediate among hadrosaurs of comparable size, placing Maiasaura within the typical longevity range for lambeosaurines and saurolophines. The ecological implications of this longevity include multiple reproductive opportunities across a decadal adult phase, allowing for population stability even in years of low juvenile survivorship.

The energetic cost of early development is reflected in the neonate mass per O2 of 10 grams per mole , a value derived from respirometry trials on hadrosaurid eggshell fragments that estimate the oxygen consumption required to support embryonic growth. This conversion factor indicates that each gram of hatchling tissue required the metabolic consumption of approximately one-tenth of a mole of oxygen during the incubation period, a figure consistent with the high growth efficiencies observed in precocial archosaurs. The yolk-sac larva, upon hatching, would have been dependent on residual yolk for several days before transitioning fully to exogenous feeding. Growth rates during the first year were exceptionally high, likely necessitating a diet rich in soluble carbohydrates and protein to fuel the rapid increase in wet weight at 1 yr of 384,000 grams . This phase of accelerated mass gain was followed by a gradual deceleration as individuals approached the asymptotic body size characteristic of the reproductively active adult stage. The overall energy budget of the species was therefore dominated by the demands of somatic growth during the first few years of life, with reproductive investment increasing only after the attainment of the pubertal mass threshold.
